assumptions: The product is sold as workflow and evidence-management software, not as legal advice, certification, or a guarantee of conformity.
Only public legal text and independently authored material are embedded unless explicit commercial standards rights are obtained.
Target advisers retain their end-client relationships and can isolate each client's confidential evidence inside the platform.
External specialist review can be purchased on a scheduled basis within the stated 30,000 PLN initial-capital estimate.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: Evidence should include the number and annual dossier volume of reachable adviser firms, paid design partners, measured hours and reviewer findings saved per dossier, renewal and per-dossier price acceptance, implementation and support effort, legal-update cost, standards licensing terms, security requirements, and independent auditor or counsel acceptance of generated packs.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: The AI Act creates recurring classification, documentation, traceability, risk, oversight, and change-management work, and packaging that work as a white-label adviser workflow is more scalable than selling founder-led legal consulting. The insight is valid but increasingly obvious: official guidance, consultancies, open templates, and governance platforms are all translating the same obligations into structured evidence processes.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Covered providers and deployers face real documentation and governance burdens, and advisers can lose billable time to inconsistent evidence collection. The chosen payer is one step removed from that pain, however; no evidence shows Polish consultancies have repeated in-scope dossier volume or will pay both an annual fee and per-dossier royalty instead of preserving their own methods, using official tools, or passing software costs directly to clients.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Annual prepayment, reusable software, and dossier usage fees can support high gross margin, fast cash conversion, and operating leverage. The 75-90% contribution target, acquisition payback, support burden, standards-license expense, legal-review cadence, retention, and 1,000-license scale are unsupported; a royalty on each dossier may also encourage advisers to bypass the product once its method is learned.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Polish compliance, quality, cybersecurity, and privacy consultancies are a clear reachable segment, and a Polish-language workflow can matter for local clients. The candidate does not size the number of adviser firms with repeated relevant engagements, distinguish currently applicable transparency or GPAI work from later high-risk-system work, or show that domestic dossier volume can support the stated wealth path.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Adviser-neutral white labeling and localized exports could win a small subsegment, but the proposed control point is authored expression and software rather than exclusive regulatory access. The European Commission now provides a free official AI Act compliance checker, while OneTrust, Credo AI, IBM, specialist consultancies, and template vendors already offer overlapping regulatory mappings, evidence workflows, and audit outputs, limiting plausible dominance without a narrower proprietary wedge.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A trusted dossier engine could extend into sector-specific packs, ISO 42001, NIST mappings, vendor assessments, continuous monitoring, audit collaboration, additional EU languages, and adjacent digital regulations. Each expansion increases legal localization and maintenance costs, but existing adviser relationships and a reusable evidence model would lower entry friction if the beachhead succeeds.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Version provenance, integrations, adviser workflow history, and consented aggregate completeness patterns could create switching costs over time. Copyright protects the implementation rather than the underlying legal requirements or workflow concept; templates and mappings are readily recreated with AI, client evidence cannot automatically be pooled, and CEN-CENELEC content requires licensing for reproduction, constraining rather than strengthening the owned asset.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Polish localization, white labeling, versioned questionnaires, validation, and export packs could reduce setup time versus spreadsheets and generic advice. No measured time saving, error reduction, reviewer acceptance, or implementation advantage is supplied, and established products already advertise automated evidence and audit outputs, so a sufficiently large behavioral or economic improvement remains plausible but unproved.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: AI Act enforcement and transparency obligations create active attention, and future high-risk obligations create a preparation window. Timing is mixed because the Commission's current timeline moves Annex III high-risk rules to 2 December 2027 and product-embedded high-risk rules to 2 August 2028, while harmonized standards remain in development; the delay reduces near-term urgency and forces costly product revisions even as it creates demand for change tracking.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: A bounded list of Polish advisory firms can be reached through direct demos, auditor relationships, and professional training, and white labeling avoids competing for their end clients. Regulatory software is trust-sensitive, the founder has no stated adviser or auditor channel, partnerships are uncommitted, and the path from founder-led sales to hundreds of economical licenses is not established.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The founder is well matched to evidence schemas, validation logic, AI-assisted development, and a low-capital software pilot. Reliable legal interpretation, standards rights, security for sensitive client evidence, professional liability boundaries, integrations, and timely updates require outside expertise and disciplined operations; these are procurable but can erode the part-time, high-margin premise.

highest_value_structural_change: Co-design a narrow, machine-verifiable dossier workflow for one high-friction AI use case with several paying Polish advisers and an independent assurance reviewer, integrate evidence capture with the client's source systems, and charge for accepted export packs and ongoing change control rather than for a broadly reusable template library alone.
main_structural_strength: Founder-owned software sold through advisers can turn recurring regulatory evidence work into prepaid, high-margin license and dossier revenue without requiring the founder to deliver every engagement.
primary_score_limiter: The addressable repeated-dossier volume and adviser willingness to pay are unverified, while the core templates and mappings are easy to reproduce and face both free official guidance and much deeper governance platforms.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: The European Commission already operates a free official AI Act Compliance Checker (https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en), and commercial incumbents advertise overlapping automated evidence and audit outputs, including OneTrust (https://www.onetrust.com/solutions/ai-governance/) and Credo AI (https://www.credo.ai/product). In addition, CEN-CENELEC states that reproduction or exploitation of standards content requires advance licensing (https://www.cencenelec.eu/european-standardization/ipr-and-patents/copyright/). Together these facts directly weaken differentiation and complicate the proposed content asset, though they do not disprove demand for a cheaper Polish adviser-specific workflow.
